key_insight: CATTS (a dynamic test-time compute allocation strategy) improves multi-step agent performance by allocating extra compute to the few hard steps where per-step errors compound, instead of uniformly increasing sampling across all steps.
problem_solved: Reduces error compounding and diminishing returns of uniform test-time scaling for agentic, long-horizon web tasks by making compute allocation adaptive to per-step difficulty.
method: Detect per-step difficulty/uncertainty (e.g., low confidence, disagreement, or low value estimates) during agent execution.
Dynamically reallocate additional inference compute (more samples, larger beam, or extra queries) to high-difficulty steps while keeping cheap processing for easy steps.
Use lightweight heuristics/predictors to decide when and how much extra compute to spend, yielding better trade-offs than uniform scaling.
impact: Practitioners get a simple, cost-effective way to boost reliability and success rates for multi-step web agents and other agentic systems without linearly increasing inference cost. CATTS enables more robust long-horizon behavior by targeting compute where it matters most.
visual_elements: Flow diagram of an agent performing multiple steps with variable compute icons showing more compute on a few hard steps (CATTS) vs equal compute per step (uniform).
Bar/line chart comparing success rate vs total inference cost: CATTS curve shows higher gains per compute than uniform scaling (diminishing returns illustrated).
Timeline illustrating error accumulation across steps and how selective extra compute interrupts compounding failures.
Icon set: confidence/uncertainty meter, compute budget meter, and a small checklist representing improved task completion
paper_authors: Nicholas Lee, Lutfi Eren Erdogan, Chris Joseph John, Surya Krishnapillai, Michael W. Mahoney
